summary:
Blink Space is a free web tool that lets anyone watch the sky change over time using images from NASA’s SPHEREx space telescope. You enter a star’s name or coordinates, and the site finds every SPHEREx visit to that spot in NASA/IPAC’s IRSA archive, cuts out a small patch from each one, aligns the frames on the sky grid, and plays them back like a flip book. Moving objects such as comets, asteroids, nearby stars and brown dwarfs show up as the one dot that jumps. The challenge asks for a public tool that makes SPHEREx’s billion-object dataset explorable by people, not only specialists. We tested the tool on all five targets from the brief using live archive data. It runs in the browser with no account, and any view can be shared as a link.

details:
Blink Space is a free web tool for watching the sky change over time with NASA’s SPHEREx telescope. Enter a star’s name or coordinates, and the site finds every SPHEREx visit to that spot in the NASA/IPAC IRSA archive, cuts out a small patch from each one, aligns the frames on the sky grid, and plays them back like a flip book. Anything that moves between visits, such as a comet, an asteroid, a nearby star or a brown dwarf, shows up as the dot that jumps.

Challenge: Planet X and SPHEREx. The brief asks for a public web tool that makes SPHEREx’s billion-object dataset easy to browse, and that handles the new data releases.

Team IWOMM: Nazar Ergeshbekov (team lead, developer), Erzhan Ermekov (developer), Kadyrbek Bolotbekov (developer), Sabina Dyushebekova (product manager).

WEB-SITE:http://iwomm.space

How it works

  1. Name or coordinates are resolved with CDS Sesame and moved to the current epoch using proper motion.
  2. SIA2 queries find every SPHEREx frame of that point in IRSA (spherex_dr1, spherex_qr3 and their deep collections).
  3. Small cutouts are downloaded, not the 70 MB full frames.
  4. Frames are reprojected onto the first frame’s WCS grid (TAN-SIP). In our live test pair, the offset dropped from 231 px to 1 px, with overlap 0.886. A 512 px frame takes about 0.15 s to align.
  5. The blink plays at 1 to 5 Hz. Advanced mode adds all 102 channels, difference images, stacks, RGB composites, spectra, Gaia and WISE overlays, and GIF/CSV/JSON export.

Two modes, one site. Simple mode is for newcomers: one band, two dates, a blink button, and an Explain button on every screen. Advanced mode is for researchers.

Honest by design. Frames are normalised independently, so brightness between blinked frames is not directly comparable, and the interface says so. The tool describes change and never claims a discovery.

Testing. We ran the tool on all five targets from the brief (Barnard’s Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855, RW Aurigae, R Draconis) on live archive data. Name lookup works for all five. The fast movers are carried to 2026 by proper motion so they stay in the field.

Stack. Next.js and React with Three.js on the frontend. A FastAPI backend split into gateway, data, image-processing and cache services, with Redis Streams for jobs and S3 for artifacts. Astropy and reproject handle the astronomy, and Aladin Lite handles sky viewing.

Limits. SPHEREx data only goes back to 2025, so the time baseline is short. Its 6.2″ pixels merge close pairs. A live cutout can take 18 to 44 seconds on the archive side, and the app shows that wait honestly. Automatic linking of moving sources across all dates is the next step
dataRefs: NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA), SPHEREx data
